analysis.one_liner: Requires new cars to detect alcohol above the legal limit and refuse to start.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote or a single cosponsor and died in committee when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Transportation Department to write a rule requiring new motor vehicles to have technology that stops the car from operating when the driver's blood alcohol is above the legal limit. It would have funded research into that detection technology, rising from $12 million a year to $20 million a year through 2027, and required states to mandate 180-day ignition interlock devices for convicted drunk drivers, withholding a growing share of federal highway funds from states that did not comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who shares the road. The bill's own findings note alcohol-impaired driving causes roughly a third of U.S. highway deaths, about 10,076 in 2013 alone, and estimates 59,000 lives and $343 billion saved over 15 years from widespread installation of detection technology [S3]. Convicted drunk drivers would face a mandatory interlock period, aimed at preventing repeat offenses [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Department of Transportation, within 10 years, to issue a safety standard that prevents a vehicle from operating when the driver's blood alcohol content is above the legal limit, with requirements that the technology be accurate, fast, unobtrusive, tamper-resistant, and easy to maintain [S2] [S3].
Funds the Driver Alcohol Detection System for Safety research program at $12 million per year in 2018-2019, $16 million in 2020-2021, and $20 million per year from 2022 through 2027 [S3].

Conditions part of federal highway money on states requiring a 180-day ignition interlock device on vehicles driven by anyone convicted of DUI, withholding 1 percent of funds in 2019, 3 percent in 2020, and 5 percent thereafter [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers would bear the cost of developing and installing the detection hardware in new vehicles, a cost likely passed to new-car buyers. States that declined to pass the interlock law would lose a share of federal highway funds, and interlock vendors would gain a new base of mandated customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Automakers, new-car buyers, and noncomplying states

drawbacks.text: The mandate would add hardware and compliance costs to every new vehicle, costs automakers would pass to buyers, and the bill set a 10-year deadline while still requiring the technology to prove itself reliable, accurate, and tamper-proof [S2] [S3].

In-vehicle alcohol detection raises practical concerns about false positives that could stop a sober driver's car, and about the privacy of continuous monitoring inside personal vehicles; the bill addresses reliability standards but leaves these questions to the rulemaking process [S2].

States face a fiscal stick: refusing the interlock mandate would cost up to 5 percent of their federal highway apportionments, effectively letting Congress override state legislative choices with money [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is enormous by the bill's own accounting — 59,000 lives and $343 billion over 15 years [S3] — against costs concentrated on new-car buyers and automakers. The design leans on technology that did not yet exist at commercial scale, so the timeline was ambitious, and the state-funding penalty is coercive. But weighing lives against hardware costs, the bill's premise is that a one-time equipment cost is a fair trade for eliminating a third of highway deaths.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and sent to subcommittees, where it sat with no hearings, no markup, no vote, and no cosponsors, and it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Kathleen Rice of New York introduced the bill on July 24, 2017 [S1] [S5].
The Speaker referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced [S5].
Within days it was routed to the Highways and Transit subcommittee and the Digital Commerce and Consumer Protection subcommittee, where no further action was ever recorded [S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor at any point in the two-year Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers avoided a federal mandate to build alcohol-detection systems into every new vehicle, and states avoided a new federal condition on their highway money. The estimated 10,000 people a year killed by drunk driving got no protection from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Kathleen Rice (D-NY)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and advocated for a federal alcohol-detection standard; recruited no cosponsors in two years.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure and Energy and Commerce Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction, routed it to subcommittees, and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor vote in the two years remaining in the Congress.

against.name: Automobile manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Would have been required to install alcohol-detection technology in new vehicles; no public congressional-record activity on this bill is available in the provided sources, though the industry's partner role in NHTSA's detection research program is documented in the bill's findings.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member, a Democrat, ever supported the bill and no Republican cosponsored it, so no meaningful partisan or bipartisan coalition ever formed — and no votes were ever taken to reveal one.

industries.note: The bill would have required alcohol-detection hardware in new vehicles, adding development and compliance costs that buyers would ultimately pay; automakers were also NHTSA's research partner on the technology the bill funds. Their interest in avoiding the mandate ran against the road-safety benefit to everyone else.

Mandatory 180-day interlock sentences for convicted drunk drivers in all 50 states would have expanded the market for breath-interlock devices; the mandate exists to keep convicted drivers off the road while impaired.
